content:
# Sirach 37 — Disagreement Log

**Chapter:** SIR 037 | **Agents:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA | **Total Disagreements:** 18

---

## Disagreement 1 — v.1: "friend" vs. "companion"

- **EMET:** "Every friend says, 'I too am a friend'"
- **LOGOS:** "Every companion says, 'I too am your friend'"
- **PNEUMA:** "Everyone calls themselves your friend"
- **Resolution (SOPHIA):** "Every companion says, 'I too am your friend'" — ἑταῖρος means "companion" (social equal, not intimate); LOGOS preserves the distinction between ἑταῖρος and φίλος (friend).

---

## Disagreement 2 — v.2: "grief even unto death" vs. "grief to the point of death"

- **EMET:** "a grief even unto death"
- **LOGOS:** "a grief to the point of death"
- **PNEUMA:** "a grief that cuts to the very heart"
- **Resolution (SOPHIA):** "a grief unto death" — the idiom is close to Mark 14:34 ("my soul is deeply grieved, unto death") and should be preserved; PNEUMA's "cuts to the heart" is vivid but obscures the hyperbolic death-reference.

---

## Disagreement 3 — v.3: "evil inclination" vs. "evil impulse"

- **EMET:** "O evil inclination!"
- **LOGOS:** "O evil impulse!"
- **PNEUMA:** "What a wretched thing is the evil impulse!"
- **Resolution (SOPHIA):** "O evil inclination!" — the Hebrew yetzer ha-ra is the classic term; "inclination" preserves the directional sense (something that tilts/bends); "impulse" is more momentary.

---

## Disagreement 4 — v.4: "false companion rejoices" vs. "two-faced companion is all smiles"

- **EMET:** "A false companion rejoices in the good fortune of a friend"
- **LOGOS:** "A false companion gloats over a friend's good fortune"
- **PNEUMA:** "A two-faced companion is all smiles when things go well for you"
- **Resolution (SOPHIA):** "A false companion rejoices in the prosperity of a friend" — "gloats" (LOGOS) implies the friend is in trouble; the verse is about feigned rejoicing in good times; PNEUMA's "all smiles" is accurate but informal.

---

## Disagreement 5 — v.5: military imagery

- **EMET:** "struggles with his friend against the belly, and in the face of the enemy takes up the shield"
- **LOGOS:** "fights alongside a friend against the enemy and stands firm against an adversary"
- **PNEUMA:** "fights alongside you against your enemies and stands by your side when the battle is fiercest"
- **Resolution (SOPHIA):** "fights alongside a friend against the enemy and takes up the shield against an adversary" — LOGOS's structure; EMET's "against the belly" is textually uncertain and possibly corrupt.

---

## Disagreement 6 — v.7: "praises counsel" vs. "gives counsel"

- **EMET:** "Every counselor praises counsel"
- **LOGOS:** "Every adviser gives advice"
- **PNEUMA:** "Every advisor is quick to give advice"
- **Resolution (SOPHIA):** "Every counselor gives counsel" — EMET's "praises" (αἰνεῖ) is what the Greek says and creates important irony (everyone praises the advice they give); LOGOS loses this. However, "gives" is more natural in English. Resolution follows LOGOS but notes the irony.

---

## Disagreement 7 — v.8: "cast the lot against you" vs. "fall upon you" vs. "steering you"

- **EMET:** "lest the counsel fall upon you"
- **LOGOS:** "lest he cast the lot against you"
- **PNEUMA:** "they may be steering you in a direction that benefits them"
- **Resolution (SOPHIA):** "lest he cast the lot against you" — LOGOS; the lot-casting image preserves the sense of a deliberate rigged outcome.

---

## Disagreement 8 — v.11: length of list

- All three include the same list with minor variations.
- Key disagreement: EMET "hired laborer for a year" vs. LOGOS "temporary worker" vs. PNEUMA "temporary hire."
- **Resolution (SOPHIA):** "hired laborer" — more literal than "temporary worker"; PNEUMA's "temporary hire" is fine but slightly informal.

---

## Disagreement 9 — v.12: "keeper of the commandments" — all agree; differ on "soul in accord"

- **EMET:** "whose soul is in accord with your own soul"
- **LOGOS:** "whose life is in harmony with your own"
- **PNEUMA:** "whose outlook is like yours"
- **Resolution (SOPHIA):** "whose soul is in accord with your own soul" — the use of ψυχή twice is meaningful and should be preserved; LOGOS substitutes "life" without warrant.

---

## Disagreement 10 — v.13: "set at nought" vs. "trust in" the heart's counsel

- **EMET:** "set at nought the counsel of your own heart" (dismissing it)
- **LOGOS:** "trust in the counsel of your own heart"
- **PNEUMA:** "listen to your own heart"
- **Note:** This is a significant interpretive disagreement. The Greek ἐν τῇ βουλῇ τῆς καρδίας σου στῆθι means "stand in the counsel of your own heart" — i.e., trust it. EMET's reading appears to follow the opposite sense.
- **Resolution (SOPHIA):** "trust also in the counsel of your own heart" — LOGOS is correct; EMET's "set at nought" misreads the verse.

---

## Disagreement 11 — v.14: "seven watchmen" vs. "seven sentinels"

- **EMET:** "seven watchmen sitting on a height"
- **LOGOS:** "seven sentinels posted on a height"
- **PNEUMA:** "seven lookouts posted on a hillside"
- **Resolution (SOPHIA):** "seven watchmen posted on a height" — "watchmen" is the traditional biblical term; "sentinels" is military; "height" is more evocative than "hillside."

---

## Disagreement 12 — v.16: "beginning" vs. "starting point"

- **EMET:** "The beginning of every work is a word"
- **LOGOS:** "The starting point of every deed is a word"
- **PNEUMA:** "Every action begins with a word"
- **Resolution (SOPHIA):** "The beginning of every work is a word" — ἀρχὴ παντὸς ἔργου λόγος; the aphoristic form ("The X of every Y is Z") should be preserved; PNEUMA's inversion loses it.

---

## Disagreement 13 — v.18: "four branches" — all agree on the phrase; differ on the tongue clause

- **EMET:** "the tongue which rules over them all has continual mastery"
- **LOGOS:** "the tongue, which governs all of them, has unceasing mastery"
- **PNEUMA:** "the tongue, which controls them all, is the master of every outcome"
- **Resolution (SOPHIA):** "the tongue, which governs them all, has unceasing mastery" — LOGOS; "governs" is more dignified than "controls" (PNEUMA) for wisdom literature; "unceasing" is better than "continual" (EMET).

---

## Disagreement 14 — v.19: "clever" vs. "wise man"

- **EMET:** "A wise man will instruct many, but he himself may be of no use"
- **LOGOS:** "There is someone who is clever and the teacher of many, yet is useless to himself"
- **PNEUMA:** "Some people are brilliant advisors to everyone else — and completely useless when it comes to helping themselves"
- **Resolution (SOPHIA):** LOGOS's "clever" is the right choice — the Greek word here (σοφός used ironically) means one who appears wise but is not truly wise; this is the key distinction Ben Sira is drawing.

---

## Disagreement 15 — v.20: "skilled in speech" vs. "eloquent"

- **EMET:** "A man skillful in speech may be hated"
- **LOGOS:** "An eloquent speaker may be hated"
- **PNEUMA:** "A polished speaker may still be despised"
- **Resolution (SOPHIA):** "A skilled speaker may be hated" — the three renderings are close; "skilled" is more neutral than "eloquent" (which implies quality) or "polished" (which implies affectation).

---

## Disagreement 16 — v.24: "call him happy" vs. "call him blessed" vs. "call him fortunate"

- **EMET:** "will call him happy"
- **LOGOS:** "will declare him fortunate"
- **PNEUMA:** "will call them fortunate"
- **Resolution (SOPHIA):** "will call him blessed" — μακαριοῦσιν is the beatitude verb; "blessed" is the proper English equivalent in religious wisdom literature, as used throughout Psalms and Proverbs.

---

## Disagreement 17 — v.25: "numbered" vs. "few"

- **EMET:** "The days of a man's life are numbered"
- **LOGOS:** "The life of a person spans few days"
- **PNEUMA:** "A person's days are few"
- **Resolution (SOPHIA):** "The days of a person's life are few" — ἐν ἀριθμῷ (lit. "in number") here means "few, countable" not "numbered by God"; LOGOS and PNEUMA are correct; EMET's "numbered" introduces a theological shade not clearly present.

---

## Disagreement 18 — v.30: "colic" vs. "stomach pain"

- **EMET:** "excess leads to colic"
- **LOGOS:** "gluttony brings on stomach pain"
- **PNEUMA:** "gorging yourself leads to stomach trouble"
- **Resolution (SOPHIA):** "gluttony brings colic" — "colic" is specific and appropriately medical; "stomach trouble" (PNEUMA) is too general.
